translations.text: Brethren, when the laws were preaching to us about mercy, and when the sermon in the assembly turned to love of the poor and to hospitality, I saw how eager all of you were. I praised your zeal and called your readiness blessed, for I looked on you as on a thirsty land, eager to seize the heavenly word.
And you know this for certain: what rain is to the earth, the word of God is to souls.
And just as rain stirs the earth to produce plants, so the word of God urges souls to bear the fruit of divinely inspired self-control.
For this reason I consider the blessed Moses a witness to the delightful and fruitful power of divine teaching. In his holy, great and honoured song of blessing he says:
"Let them wait for my speech as for rain, and let my words come down like dew."
And so that no one should think he attributed the abundance of such divine speech to himself, he immediately adds: “For I will proclaim the name of the Lord.”
I praise you, brethren, because you are not only eager to hear the words, but you also store up in yourselves the beauty of their meaning, like the wise bee.

Having entered the immortal and spiritual meadows of the holy Scriptures, and gardens decked with the flowers of piety, each of you makes the honey of the divine oracles in the hidden hives of the soul.
Just as the bee and the nature and strength of bees come from flowers, and enjoyment must come from the bees’ labors,

In the same way, the flower and the power of piety come from the divine Scriptures, and the enjoyment of piety comes from the labour of the virtuous. Such a one has made in the soul honeycomb [?] of the divine oracles.
And the blessed David, having tasted how great a good piety is, cried aloud in the strains of the psalms:
"Your words are sweet to my palate, sweeter than honey to my mouth."
Yet I do not so much praise your eagerness as I marvel at our father's freedom from envy. He has blossomed with divine love and has been made radiant by heavenly graces.
He waters the church so abundantly and in such a way, and gladdens this city of God. This is a fitting moment to quote the words of the Psalm: "The streams of the river make glad the city of God."
He pours out such holy and clear streams, yet he does not scorn the few drops of our words. Such a cloud, [?] with heavenly rains, does not [?] to receive the faint splashing of our tongue.
Instead he joins you in giving praise. Even before you, through the intercession of his holy prayers, he grants us who speak the power to speak, and grants the hearers eagerness to listen.

He praises what is his own as though it were another's, and so imitates his Lord Christ. Christ took up the words of the prophets and praised the preaching of the prophet. He himself spoke through the mouth of the prophet Isaiah, and he himself sounded forth the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

Yet he treated his own words as if he had received them from the prophet, and said to the Jews: "Hypocrites, Isaiah spoke well about you." It was not Isaiah who spoke well; rather, you spoke well through Isaiah, and through all the prophets.
And Zechariah bears witness to this: "As he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets."
It was not the mouths of the prophets, but the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Just as a reed pen writes not what it wishes, but what the hand commands,

In the same way, the tongue of the prophets did not speak what it wished, but what the power of the Holy Spirit commanded. That is why David's cry is rightly considered fitting: "My tongue is like the pen of a swift scribe."
And now may this wondrous father himself, through his holy prayers, grant us an abundance of words; may he hear and praise the very thing that prayer gives.
And now, since we have such a father, and since the feast is also beginning,
come, helped by his holy prayers, let us fly up and lift our minds to the height of the glory of the Only-begotten.

We do this not in order to grasp anything of the majesty of his honour, but so that we may hasten in love to reach him. For nothing can grasp the honour of the Only-begotten: neither broad words nor [?] of minds. It goes far beyond every mind and every thought.

The blessed David said this in a figure: "A man will approach a deep heart, and God will be exalted." The more anyone ponders words about God, the higher above him he finds the knowledge of the truth.

And now let us speak about the kindness of the Only-begotten, drawing on the present reading. The fountain of wisdom makes use of parables, as he said through the mouth of David: “I will open my mouth in parables.”
And he tells an example and a parable full of power, which, judging by its words, seems to contain nothing resembling his goodness.
“Which of you has a friend and goes to him at midnight and says, ‘Friend, give me three loaves of bread, for a friend of mine has arrived from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’?
“And he will answer and say: ‘The doors are shut, and my children are with me in bed. Do not trouble me; I cannot get up and give it.’” And what did he give that man?
“Amen, I say to you: even if he will not give because of friendship, yet because of his persistence he will get up and give him more than he wanted. And I say to you: ask, and you shall receive.”
And what likeness to his kindness does the parable present?

For he is sleepless by nature, while this man lies drowsing in bed. He is not overtaken by sluggishness, while this man is a slave to sluggishness and sleep. So what does that likeness in the parable mean to show?
And he adds to the same: “You too, ask,” just as that man persisted in asking the sleeper. Do you too sleep, then?
Did not the prophets cry out about you that the guardian of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps? So what does this likeness in your parable mean to make clear?
The words of the Life-giver regularly set forth like things by means of like things, and show opposites by means of their opposites. He makes this clear in the other parable as well,

when, on one occasion, he wished to set forth by means of the opposite his abundantly flowing kindness, his plentiful and overflowing graces, and his inexhaustible generosity, and he brought forward an example of this kind, just as we have now heard.
But first let this be examined and made clear: what does he mean to show? For even though the example is not alike,

the Saviour means to say this: the man who was a slave to sleep, overcome by sluggishness, and unwilling behind his closed doors was urged by the persistent asker to hold out and to give him enough. By endurance, the asker's pleading won out.

How much more will the nature that is free of sluggishness (God, I mean), who is not moved by pleading and is no slave to sleep, be moved to hold out and satisfy those who persist and who begin in truth! And who is there who would wage war and fight against such a mind?

And so that you may learn for certain that he taught a thing by means of its opposite: coming down a little further, he uses the same kind of example, so that he may show a thing by means of its opposite.
“Which of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will he give him a snake instead of the fish?
Or if he asks for an egg, will he give him a scorpion instead of the egg?” And when he had spoken of the better things by comparison with human beings,
he then says: “For if you, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father, the heavenly Father, give good things to those who ask him.”
Do you see how, by comparing something with its opposite, he demonstrated the opposite of it?
He also uses a parable of this kind elsewhere, as I said earlier. I consider it important to explain what it is and what force it has.
“There was a judge,” he says, “in a certain city, who did not fear God and was not ashamed before people.
And a widow kept pleading with him persistently, and he never settled anything for her.” For because of his harshness and his failure to know God, he would not give in to her pleas and entreaties.
But her persistence overcame his merciless harshness. The unjust judge says to himself:
“Though I do not fear God and am not ashamed before people, at least because she troubles me I will grant her justice.” This is the parable he tells.
But the Life-giver wished to show a thing by means of its opposite, and he immediately adds after it [?]: “See,” he says, “what the unjust judge said.”

If the persistence, endurance and perseverance of the widow brought the unjust and merciless god [? read: judge] to consent, will not persistence, endurance and perseverance bend the sweet and most compassionate Father and the Lord who loves mankind to entreaty and mercy? This he showed by this parable; and the same he discourses on now as well.
And I say to you: ask, and you shall receive; knock, and it shall be opened to you.
Follow the example of the friend who knocked at the door and said, “Friend, open to me.” You too should knock, and it will be opened. Seek, and you will find.
But when you ask of God, consider what one ought to ask, and from what kind of one.
For many hold all sorts of opinions about God in prayer: when they entreat on account of their own sins, they want God to be sweet and loving toward mankind;
and when they call for vengeance on those who have wronged them, they want him harsh and severe and a just judge.
When someone stands in prayer on his own behalf, he sets forth words of entreaty and supplication which can persuade God:
"I beseech you," he says, "Lord, have mercy on me, unworthy as I am; you are sweet, beneficent, and loving toward mankind, you who do not look upon sins and overlook transgressions.
If you should mark iniquities, who could endure before you? Deal with me according to your mercy."
All this they say when they offer prayers on their own behalf. But when someone, grieved by an enemy, comes to stand in prayer, he forgets such words and turns his supplications to another mind:
"Lord," he says, "you are a just judge, and evil deeds are not pleasing to you."
Take vengeance on my enemies, for you are a righteous judge. Do not be patient with those who oppress me, but, as a just judge, demand justice.”
When I judge you, you want me sweet and beneficent; and when I judge your enemy, just and impartial. Have you forgotten your first prayers?

Did you not call upon me as sweet? Did you not seek to persuade me as one who loves mankind? Did you not beseech me as long-suffering? How then? Must I divide myself according to your wishes, and sell justice for your pleasure?
No, it is not possible for you to find only good things from my beneficence, and for your enemies to find only sentences of justice from my just judgment;
for the beneficent one is beneficent toward all. Perhaps, while you stand in prayer against your enemies, you provoke the Judge to anger against yourself. How so?
The just judge examines your case and another person’s equally. If you invoke him as a just judge against your enemies, you must also stir the judge up against yourself.
But if you appeal to him as a benefactor on your own behalf, then he will be a benefactor to everyone, even if you do not wish it.
Therefore, anyone who stands in prayer must ask for what is pleasing to God. It is fitting to ask for whatever God takes pleasure in.
For if the Savior, when he said, “Father, if it is at all possible, let this cup pass from me,” immediately added,
“But not as I will, but as you will,” do you, an unruly man, choose your own wishes instead of taking refuge in his will?
But now let us bring the discourse to this point. For I know that this is precisely what you were asking for, and I see you crowded together, cramped, and eager to hear the discourse.
But take comfort, for Isaiah has arrived and will give you encouragement: “Bear with these hardships, you who are eager to listen.”
He spoke well; and listen well, all of you, who are pressed together, made spacious, eased in spirit;
for this pressure here will become for you relief from many afflictions. Those who endure sweat in themselves for God's sake dispel all the pains of sins;
for if the sweat that is produced by the body dispels pains, then such sweat as, for the sake of God and his messages, from a fountain of longing —
which you have come forward to hear — they pour forth, will it not indeed wash away all sins at once?

But let us go on to what lies before us; for I know that you are demanding the remnants of the discourse. Many, longing for it as for friends, seek it, and hunt for many pretexts, and think to reject [?].
For the disparagement of the many who wish to find fault with us has not escaped our notice: they say that we left the discourse incomplete, without examining the matter.
But I am astonished at such people, not at their slander but at their untimeliness. You find fault as though you had made a loan and had not received repayment.
When you asked for the discourse, was I [?] about giving the explanation? Did someone else put the question forward, and did I reject it?
I made the promise of my own accord, and I myself forgot. If that is so, blame the frailties of my nature, and do not reproach the exposition of the discourse.
For even if the occasion [?] had passed us by, even so the weakness of my speech would not have destroyed the force of the inquiry; for the rights of truth are not banished by my incapacity,

since the reasons for the matters before us are indeed evident; but the abundance of the words already spoken has sifted the mind this way and that, so that it drifted away from the inquiry that lay before us.
And now, what I left unfinished unwillingly then, I will willingly repay now as a debt.

And even when I repay the debt, I am again apprehensive, for I see in you a new and marvelous drunkenness — a drunkenness that does not [? text: ո'ճ] drive the mind into stupor, but rouses the memory more and more. And that the effect of drunkenness is to stupefy the mind, you all know.
But you, brothers, the more you become intoxicated with the divine word, the more you drive dullness away from your attention and plant divine memories in its place.
And this indeed is marvelous: that cupbearers, becoming drunk, grow heavy from the abundance of their serving, and you, who have drained so many vessels [?] of the divine word,
And after the drunkenness you are thirsty, and you insistently demand the leftovers. It is truly right to hear the words of those who drink spiritually. "Where is the cup?" they say.
"The cup was left over. He did not explain the cup. He did not pay what he owed on the words about the cup."

I love you, who have longed for the cup of Christ. I love you, who ask for what is left over. I love you, who, for the sake of this beautiful drunkenness, do not want to lose even one cup. And you are quite right to do so.

For at bodily feasts, a person who passes up one cup out of modesty is admired. But at the divine rejoicing and at the heavenly table, a person who leaves nothing of the things that bring on drunkenness in [?]…
Rather, the one who is at once satisfied and hungry, drunk and thirsty, is the one who will truly be filled with eternal salvation.
And now blessed are those who speak and those who hear. The hearers are blessed because they thirst to hear,
as the Savior also says: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled."
And the speakers are blessed because they sound the divine teaching into living ears. Blessed are those who speak into the ears of those who listen.
And now let us come to the text.
"Father," he says, "if it is possible, let this cup pass from me."

This text is full of many questions, and it causes the heretics a great deal of serious harm. The harm does not come from the text saying anything evil, but from their wrong understanding of the phrase "if it is possible."

Some supposed that certain unfailing decrees, which could not be transgressed, were proclaimed from the body [?]: namely, fate and allotment and the necessity attached to what is fabulously called one’s nativity, as though something were thus allotted to each person from birth.

And some dishonor the dignity of the Only-begotten in another way: they fasten a slavish obedience of the Son to the Father onto him. For, they say, he was under the Father’s authority, and for that reason he offered such supplications.

What argument is suitable for us to resolve these questions? What thoughts will suffice to unravel the many-voiced fables of the heretics? It would not be possible [?] to learn from anywhere else than from the truth itself.
Come, then, let us run up to the divine heights, there to the economy of the Life-giver on high,
who does everything and says everything not only according to the honor that befits him, but also according to the economy that suits us.
And to cut it short (for I always like to keep things short and to cover much in few words): the Life-giver knew beforehand that the sufferings were absolutely necessary.
He knew beforehand that the cross is set up for the salvation of the world, that death is rebuked, and that resurrection is provided.

And he knew this so well that he told the disciples beforehand, “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered into the hands of sinners, and they will scourge him and crucify him, and on the third day he will rise.”
This is the utterance of God, who knows future things beforehand. It is God who anticipates the actual experience of events; it is God who directs human affairs with knowledge.
Then Peter answers him about this, moved with pity for his body: “Far be it, Lord,” he says. “Let this not happen to you.”

And what did the Life-giver do about this? He was angry at the ill-timed compassion; he rebuked the untimely concern: "Get behind me, Satan, for you are not thinking the things of God, but those of men." This fits the text well.

And you, examine this closely and be on your guard. For if you are a slave to the bare words, you will overturn much concerning the Life-giver. You will slander him with charges not only of weakness but also of wavering in his purposes.

O good Lord, when Peter wished, "Far be it from you that you should go up to the cross," you reproached him. And now do you yourself beg for the very thing you blamed him for? That would not befit even a steadfast man, let alone [?].

Who would praise a general who makes many promises before the battle and boldly shouts defiance at the enemy, but turns to flight when the battle lines clash and disgraces his strength through cowardice?

Before Christ came to his sufferings, he said to the one who was trying to keep him from them: "Get away from me, Satan, for you are not thinking the things of God, but those of men." Would he who judged such thoughts unworthy of God then take up those same thoughts himself and pray for that very thing?

Oh, the folly, or rather the arrogance, of those who are slaves to the bare words! They dare everything rashly and presume to interpret divine things in a way other than what is meant. They do not want to recognize that by taking only the bare words,
they show him not only lower than the Father, as they are eager to do, but also inferior to many wise and righteous men, and lacking even ordinary human steadfastness.
What wise or righteous person, or indeed any human being whose courage is attested, would deny his own virtue and dishonor the strength he had promised and previously boasted of?
Who would behave so cowardly and inopportunely as to dare and undertake one thing, but think another and shrink back when put to the test?
He who threatened death with death and proclaimed the good news of the resurrection—how could he himself shrink from the cross?
I have said all this to rebuke those who serve words, dishonor the Lord, and sell the truth.
Now, what would anyone wish to demonstrate against the contradiction between the words, when the truth is always found to agree with itself?
And what agreement with the truth could anyone find in a fight over words? Words do indeed fight with one another, but the harmony of the divine oracles stays firm.
Now I must explain the solution to the question before us with a diligent disposition, and you must listen with minds eager to learn.
When the Lord drew near to the crucifixion, to the fulfillment of the whole economy,
the blessed and only Mighty One, the King of kings and Lord of lords, knew beforehand that many heretics would rise up against the truth,

and they would separate off the divine sufferings and falsely declare the deeds foreign to him; and especially those who share in the name of error, I mean the disciples of the Manichaeans, who even dared to say
that Christ's sufferings were a kind of shadow and an illusion before the eyes, as though he had not even taken a body, and the cross was only an appearance,

and the body was some shadow and likeness, and indeed everything that was carried out in the dispensation was appearance, shade [?], illusion, and something seen only by the eyes. It was because of this heretical error, I mean that of the disciples of the Manichaeans, that he wanted to shut the mouths of the heretics in advance and make it clear that he put on this body, which is subject to many sufferings. You who shrink from sufferings, who tremble at the violence of death, who are troubled and tremble at the end of life:
“Now,” he says, “my soul is troubled.” And again: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.”

And again: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” If these things were shadow, a sight before the eyes, and illusion, why was he troubled? If the things being done were only some kind of appearance, why did he shrink from them?
For no one is afraid of a shadow, and no one is troubled by mere appearances.
Would you like me also to demonstrate the truth more firmly from an account of ours? Angels entered Sodom. In appearance they looked like men, but by nature they were angels.
The Sodomites dared to force them, as though they were men, into filthiness and into unworthy wickedness. But now, what did the angels do?

Because they knew that they had no body that could be subjected to violence, they were not troubled. Instead, the nature of the angels stayed without disturbance and suffered no turmoil from the [?] of the body's passions.
But Lot, because he considered them righteous men, was troubled lest they suffer some violence. He pleaded with those raging men:
“I beg you,” he says, “do no wrong to these men, since they have come in under my roof.

I will give you my offspring. Take my daughters and do whatever you wish.” O fervent hospitality! He was ready to give his own in place of others, as a payment of debt [?]. Lot, being a man, was troubled,
but the nature of the angels suffered no disturbance.

For they came out with great power and snatched away him who could have suffered violence, and they struck with blindness those who were raging with such great and frenzied fury, or rather with such godless shamelessness.
They wandered about all night, looking for the door, but could not find it. For those who used their sight for evil were rightly and justly blinded.

And why was all this said, since the preceding discussion has nothing in common with the present one? It was to show that where there is an outward appearance, there is no fear, but where there is a real body, there are fear and sorrow.

But so that the Life-giver might make it entirely clear for what reason he had spoken the word, he cut off the thinking of the heretics, planted the religion of truth, and said to the apostles: “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.” He counts the weakness as belonging to his flesh, yet you throw the sufferings onto his divinity. But if you do not hurry to find the sense of the word, you will be found to have insulted the Lord.
For you not only establish what you suppose—that he offered prayers to the Father, and that the one who prays is inferior to the one whom he entreats—but I will say something still clearer:
If you attend only to the words, you make him inferior not only to the Father but even to his own apostles.
Just as they badly misinterpret the saying, “I speak nothing on my own, but my Father gave me a command about what I should say and what I should speak,” so they also misinterpret this.
Here let apostolic authority come forward on my behalf and silence the mouths of these madmen.
Paul says, “Concerning virgins, I have no command from the Lord, but I give advice.” And he shows that the heretics’ teachings are truly very base.
If Paul has authority to act freely without a command from God, does Christ not have authority to speak without the Father’s commands?

So also here, to show the heretical error by comparing it with apostolic courage, coming [?] to claim that the Lord's utterance is far lower than the apostolic dignity. But as I have said many times before, if you are a slave only to the words, nothing more is achieved.
But if we grasp their meaning, the truth remains undefiled—or rather, we ourselves remain undefiled, for the truth is never [?].

Now, if you pay no attention to the interpretation but attend only to the words, you will find Christ losing courage and speaking in a way far beneath not only his own dignity but also the apostles’ courage.
For Christ says, “Now my soul is troubled.” And when Paul went to the regions of Palestine, a prophet named Agabus came there and said:
“Thus says the Holy Spirit: The man whose girdle this is, the Jews will bind in this way in Jerusalem.” And when all the brethren were holding Paul back and begging him not to go to Jerusalem,

he answered with a voice of courage, or rather, with a spirit of courage and apostleship, he said to those who were holding him back: “What are you doing? Why do you weep and crush my heart within me?
For I am ready not only to be bound but also to die for the name of Christ.”
Paul speaks with such confidence, such boldness, such fearlessness [?], and tramples underfoot, despises, and [?] the terrors of death.
Yet Paul’s Lord said, “Now my soul is troubled.” Paul’s heart was being crushed, but was Christ troubled in his very soul?
Paul even boasted in his afflictions: “Not only this, but we also boast in our afflictions,
because we know that afflictions produce endurance.” Yet Christ, Paul’s Lord, said, “My soul is sorrowful to the point of death.” What resemblance is there to boasting?
Paul regarded his sufferings as a reason for boasting. Yet did Christ, who strengthened him, regard the dispensation as a cause for sorrow?
Consider also, elsewhere, Paul's thoughts, and how they are entirely full of courage.

[?] once remained in the city of the Philippians, in the land of the Macedonians. A great crowd rose up against him, and he bore all kinds of tortures in his body. After laying many blows on him, they threw him into prison and fastened his feet in the stocks.
But the valiant champion of devotion to God, and Silas, who was with him, overcame their pains through steadfastness and conquered their sufferings through courage.
The one who wrote the history noted this well, saying: "At midnight Paul and Silas were praising God."
They are afflicted, and they give thanks; they were taking blows [?], and they were praising. And see the precision of the one who wrote the history.
He did not say that at midnight Paul and Silas offered prayers to God, but that they were praising. Prayers perhaps come from distress of heart, and praise from joy of heart.
So you see that the apostles were showing joy. "At midnight," he says, "Paul and Silas were praising God." Praise is a sign of rejoicing souls.
The saints, wishing to make the gladness of their souls plain, did not offer prayers like people in distress, but praised like people set free.
Paul and Silas, who were men by nature,

showed virtuous spirits in their sufferings. And do you apply godless words to Christ, who is King of the saints? Do you take what was said for the sake of the divine plan as an attack on his honour? Away with you, get rid of such thoughts!
Let no one dishonor holy things; let no one slander the divine words; let no one strive to construct impiety from the words of the Giver of life, or regard the dispensation as a downfall.
But the listener asks us for an orderly explanation. “You have taught us well,” he says. “The words were indeed part of the dispensation. But explain also the actual significance of the dispensation.
Why did he use such words at all? Why did he say, ‘If it is possible, let this cup pass from me’?”
"If it be possible," brethren, does not bring in any necessity imposed by command, or the fabled name of fate,

and these are not words of faint-heartedness. Nor should the speaker be slandered on that account as if he were shrinking back. Rather, they were the outward form of the human plan of salvation, and of sparing those who would stumble. For he knew that the sufferings could make many stumble, especially those who were not versed in the mysteries of the plan of salvation.
According to the saying, “We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles.”
Now he who manages everything with wisdom, speaking on behalf of humanity, said, “If it is possible to fulfill the saving plan in another way and complete it without death,”
so that many might not stumble because of such sufferings: “If it is possible, let this cup pass from me.”

"But you are twisting the words," they say. "Come, show some testimony that bears witness to the truth, that he said this on account of human weakness and [?]." If that is what you want, listen: how was he able, right then and there, to say to the apostles:
"Keep praying, keep awake"? And when they fell asleep, he reproached them and said: "So, could you not keep watch with me for one hour?

Keep praying, so that you do not enter into temptation." He did not say, "so that I do not enter," because the sufferings did him no harm. Rather, they would make others stumble. "Keep praying, so that you do not enter into temptation."
He did not say, “So that we do not enter,” but, “So that you do not enter.” “I am sparing you; it is not that I wish to save myself from the sufferings.”
“I know what is to come. I am not ignorant of the saving plan that is to be fulfilled. I am no novice concerning the blessing that is to blossom for all humanity.”
“But because, even before these events take place, what you see causes you to stumble, I speak in your words: ‘If it is possible for the sufferings to pass, let them pass.’”
The words must be repeated twice and three times, to make clear that there is a possibility, not something inevitable in nature that cannot be bypassed, or an unavoidable decree, as some thought.

Do you want to hold firmly that there was no necessity or limit laid from above on the Life-giver, but that this is his own all-knowing plan, and that he accomplishes everything by his own will? Then listen carefully
to how the Lord himself removed the idea of necessity beforehand and made clear the sovereignty of his will.
“No one takes my life from me,” he says. “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again.” And again: “Destroy this temple, and I will raise it up on the third day.”
And if you have authority, why do you utter such words? “If it is possible,” you say, “let this cup pass from me.”
“I say this for your sake, you who are weak, and not for my own sake, for I am strong and almighty, above and beyond every weakness.”
But why did he call the sufferings a cup? From this another question also presents itself: why did he call the sufferings a cup?
"Yes," he says, "it is always the custom of Scripture to call the chastisement that comes from God on transgressors a 'cup'."
Pay careful attention and be a wise listener. Do not snatch at the words too quickly. Listen, and wait for the meaning.

Someone who listens maliciously can interpret what is said maliciously. Yet one who speaks in church should not think it strange if he suffers slander from those who rashly and without cause turn to calumny. The apostles too were slandered, as though they had said something improper.
Listen to Paul, and see how much slander he endured in his preaching: "And why not, as we are blasphemed and as some report that we say, 'Let us do evil so that good may come'?"
"Their condemnation is just." For they slander what they never heard as if they had heard it. What they did not hear from the teachers, they put forward as a slander against the teachers.
But let us return to the matter before us. It is always a distinctive practice of Scripture to call the chastisements or punishments that come upon sinners a cup.

But let no enemy or spy quickly carp at these words and say, "Did Christ also sin, then, that he should bear the punishments of sinners?" Far be it from us to say that. He owed no punishment at all. Away with that idea, [?].
But we were under punishment.
And for our sake, condemned as we were for sins and liable to punishment and torment, he took death upon himself. As Isaiah had already proclaimed and announced, he came to death for us sinners.
And that he personally accepted death on account of the punishments of sinners, let the Baptizer bear witness: “Behold the Lamb of God,
who takes away the sins of the world.” And the prophet says, “He bears our sins and suffers for us,” and, “Because of the sins of the people he came to death.”
His sufferings are called a cup, according to the words quoted earlier. For that very reason, blessed David also speaks figuratively of the punishments that will come upon sinners:
"A cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed wine, mixed; all the sinners of the earth shall drink."
And again, when God himself was threatening the nations with punishment, he said to Jeremiah:
"Take the mixed cup and give it to all the nations to drink, and to Jerusalem; and say to them, 'Drink, and be drunk, and be stupefied.'" What does "be stupefied" mean?
That chastisement drives many into stupefaction, and often even into astonishment, especially when they see the righteous caught along with the sinners.
So even now people throughout the whole earth complain, "Why were the priests slaughtered at the altars?"
Why were the holy virgins handed over to abuse? For what reason were so many evils committed, and on such a scale? Why did God not protect his own?”
And because such afflictions bring people into a daze and bewilder their minds, he rightly says, “Drink, become foolish, and run wild.”
Again, when the giver of life spoke beforehand to James and John about his sufferings, he said, “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?”
This was instead of saying, “Can you bear the sufferings that I am going to bear?” And they said, “Yes.”
But in another place blessed David showed plainly that a death that comes upon someone for the sake of godliness is called a cup:

"What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has given me?" Like a deeply grateful servant, he saw God's benefits pouring out all around him, and he himself seeks to give some small return, with a willing mind, for those boundless benefits. Likewise, when a poor man brings a rich man to his lodging, he falls into perplexity about what preparations he could make to please the rich man,

and about what he could bring to the table that would be worthy of the man's rank. He would stand there at a loss and say to himself, "What worthy thing could I find for him? What shall I do? What shall I set before him? How shall I honour him? What kind of meal could I prepare?"
In the same way, David looked at human poverty and the greatness of divine generosity, and saw that there was nothing worthy that a human being

…the one who would approach God fell into perplexity. He was at a loss, and he [?] spoke, saying, "What shall I render to the Lord? I find nothing worthy of his benefits. What shall I render to the Lord? What sort of person should I become? What offerings shall I give? With what [?] shall I win the favour of my benefactor?"

Finding himself destitute of everything, he found only one thing. Even that is not worthy of God's beneficence, but it is worthy of his own willingness: "I will receive the cup of salvation." What is this cup?
"If I am able," he says, "to endure sufferings for the sake of godliness, if I am found capable of dying for God: I will receive the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord."
And since the saying was not plain but veiled and abbreviated, he explains it with what follows.
I will receive the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord. He adds alongside this: Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.
And now, what does this saying mean: Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass? Is it not clear that he was speaking of his sufferings?
But you have already been given the answer to your question: by saying, “If it is possible,” he fulfills the human aspects of the dispensation.
For the one who said this according to his humanity had himself already said according to his all-powerful divinity: I have authority to lay down my life,
and I have authority to take it up again. And he makes it clear that it was not his divinity that shrank from the sufferings, but the weakness of his flesh.

And again he says, "The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak." This was not because the sufferings would do him any harm, but because they would cause others to stumble. And he showed this to the disciples:

"Stand in prayer," he says, "so that you may not enter into temptation." In another way, too, he hands down to us a rule for prayer: we should not insist at all that God grant the things we ask for in our prayers, but should take refuge in him who governs all things with wisdom.
For indeed he says, "Not as I will, but as you will." What was fitting for him is also entirely appropriate for you.
So when you stand in prayer, do not ask for whatever you yourself wish, but take refuge in God's will.
You too, when you stand in prayer, should speak in imitation of Christ, who humbled himself for your sake:
Not as I will, but as you will, Lord. Take refuge in God's will. Do not give him instructions, and do not regard yourself as his adviser.

For those who love God, he says, everything succeeds and will work together for their good. Whatever accords with his will is accomplished, and whatever is outside his will does not come to completion.
The cup of God's chastisement comes upon sinners as punishment. But for Christ, the sufferings were not punishment, but providence, for he endured the death of sinners without sin,
…so that he might save the whole world, which had been condemned under sin.
Why, he says, does he call death a cup at all? The testimonies of the Scriptures themselves have shown plainly that punishments and death are called a cup.
But why were sufferings called a cup at all, since a cup is in no way like death?
Because the chastisements that come upon us are harsh, unbearable, and difficult, the divine Scriptures call these afflictions a cup by analogy,
so that it may be clear that God does not torment like a harsh judge or slaughter without mercy, but heals our ailments like a physician and gives us chastisements to swallow like [?] of potent gall.
Thus the saving cup of chastisement is bitter to taste but beneficial for healing. The passage presents God as a benefactor,
who disciplines with the cup, who is benevolent like a father, and who torments and punishes like a king. He does not strike like an enemy, but causes pain like a physician.
For example, when a physician uses an iron instrument and applies cauterization to the body, he is not thereby fighting against the person, but battling the ailments.
Likewise, when God brings chastisements, he does not punish his creation, but cleanses its sins.
Have you ever seen a physician put his hand to work out of wrath, or resort to cauterization out of anger, or do anything else of the kind?
Even though the physician's face may seem terrifying to the sick person, the physician has the patient's benefit in mind.
And not because the pain-causing treatment may seem dreadful, or the promise of medical skill may be something dreadful.
Thus the blessed Paul has rightly and wonderfully set out a rule for discipline, saying, “All discipline, for a time, seems to bring not joy but sorrow.”

When a wounded man sees that the physician wants to cut [?] the wound, he is terribly [?] and flees from him as from an enemy. But once he is healed, he afterwards looks closely at the one he once saw and turned his face away from, and he bows down before him.

Do we not know that, in their anger at their pain, the sick insult their physicians, and the physician bears with those who are angry? For he knows that their insults are not deliberate, but arise from their pain.
But when they recover from their illness, they even pay those whom they considered cruel. They pay not because payment is demanded, but willingly and gladly.
In the same way, we too are now reluctant to endure afflictions; but when the fruit of those afflictions comes, then we praise our benefactor,
and in wonder we say with David, “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into rest.”
Now he calls afflictions a cup—and not simply a cup, but one in the Lord’s hand, full of unmixed wine, yet mixed.
Again, the words seem to contain a contradiction, for mixed and unmixed are not at all alike.
So why is the cup both unmixed and mixed? Because God's judgment and the chastisement that comes upon us is unmixed, and the mixed is unmixed. What is the mixture?
With justice there is equity; and neither lawlessness, nor injustice, nor any doubt is mixed with justice.

Rather, its nature [?] is truly unmixed. The eye of judgment is holy and clear, righteously vigorous and luminous, keen-sighted, swift [?] in inquiry, upright in action, weighing all things, impartial. That is why there is a cup of unmixed wine in the hand of the Lord.
For injustice is not mixed with justice, and none of the adversaries there could bring doubt into the truth of the judge.

For there is a cup of unmixed wine in the hand of the Lord. And if it is of unmixed wine, how can it be full and mixed? Do not let the words seem to contradict each other; the truth brings them into agreement.
The cup is unmixed, as I have already said many times, because injustice is not mixed with righteousness; and it is mixed because love for humanity is also mixed with righteousness.
It is as though he were saying that it is pure in righteousness and mixed with love for humanity, for in disciplining he shows mercy, and in showing mercy he disciplines.

And see another new definition of the truth. When God chastises sinners, it is a sign of his providence and his love for humankind. When he does not chastise the transgressor, it is a sign of goodness and wrath.

Then it is fearful [?], as though he hated you and turned his face away, when you transgress and he does not chastise you. "Whom the Lord loves," it says, "he punishes; he scourges every son whom he receives."
From such a person, because of the great number of his sins, he turns his face away and leaves him without chastisement and punishment.

And who makes this plain? God himself, through the prophet: "Because you have transgressed my laws," he says, "I will not punish your daughters when they commit fornication, nor your brides when they commit adultery." It is as if he were saying:
"I will hand you over to your sins. I will not punish the iniquity, I will not restrain the corruption, I will not heal the wounds of your transgressions,
but I will let you die right there in your evils." See how, when he is angry, he threatens not to chastise; and when he truly loves, he does not hold back from chastising.
Brethren, it has not yet been shown, as far as we are able, what kind of prayer that was, and what he wished to show by saying, "Father, if it is possible,
let this cup pass from me." For such words do not come from his divine majesty but from his human dispensation,
And the Lord himself made it still clearer that I attribute the more humble words—those of fear, turmoil, and sorrow—to the weakness of the flesh.

so that it might be confirmed that he truly took a body capable of suffering. "The spirit," he says, "is willing, but the flesh is weak." I remind you [?] of this saying many times so that I may establish your minds in the truth.
Then, if anyone dares to dispute the solution to the question that we have given, let him come forward, take his stand, and fight against our arguments,
if he is capable of waging war against the divine word. Let him not [?] like an enemy, but let him fight openly, like a champion battling for the truth.

But let this be enough for now. We have come back to what was said at the beginning, and there let us rest the discourse. It seems to me that the pattern of the dispensation and the interpretation of this saying have been shown completely and fully. For if anyone still argues against it after so much testimony, the truth is not sullied by that in any way.
As Paul also says, “If anyone wishes to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the church of God.”
For we have learned from the Scriptures to believe, not to chew the cud of speculation. And I pray to go astray with [?], rather than display cleverness with Plato.
Let what has been said be enough and sufficient for us, and let us only remember the poor. Concerning this, Paul also rightly reminded us today:

“Peter, James, and John gave the right hand of fellowship to me and Barnabas, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcised.” And he immediately added to this, “Only let us remember the poor.”
Let us also remember the poor; let us remember the poor so that we may remember ourselves.
If you show mercy to another, you show mercy to yourself.
You do good to yourself if you do good to the poor. You sow for yourself and reap for yourself. Mercy is sown here, and kindness is reaped in heaven.
And do not say, “What can I do? I am bound by poverty. I wish to show mercy, but I lack the means. I desire to do good, but the scarcity of my resources does not allow it.”
Do as much as you can. Perform good deeds to the extent that you have the means.
Learn not only to listen eagerly [?], but also, you who are eager [?], to show mercy.
And listen to Isaiah: "If you give bread to the hungry from your heart." What does "from your heart" mean?

It means "from what you yourself were going to eat." If you take it and give it and make the poor man share your food, you have shown mercy to yourself by feeding him. Do you remember, perhaps? I know that you also remember what was said earlier about almsgiving.
Mercy brings about friendship with God. Mercy brings forgiveness of sins. Mercy saves from death.

There was the blessed Tabitha, who was handed over to death by the law of nature, and who came back again from death to life through the thanksgiving of the widows, because the tears of the poor broke open the gates of death. Pay attention:
how much the prayers of the poor man [?] are able [?] to accomplish.
When Tabitha died, who was full of good works, all the widows came and stood around Peter and wept.

And the tears of the poor eased the mourning. More than that, they even overcame the tyranny of death, for she who had died according to the laws of nature came back by the word of grace. She was full of almsgiving and good works; the widows wept, and they moved God to entreaty.
Dying is according to our nature, and raising up is outside and above our nature.

For if the tears of the needy could accomplish what is outside our nature, will they not be able to accomplish what is according to nature? Consider how powerful the complaints of a widow are when she complains against a rich man. If a poor man complains against a great man who oppresses him, if an orphan complains against the powerful, what kind of vengeance will be carried out?
Let the poor man not complain against you, and let the needy man not groan, and let the orphan not lament and raise an outcry against you.
Instead, sow mercy among orphans, so that you may store up kindness for your own children.
Be an imitator of Abraham, who spread compassionate kindness among all who were in need and left his descendants a pledge of salvation.
And see the wonderful thing: because of the honor he showed through hospitality, he was found worthy to receive even the angels of God.
He received the angels with hospitality, thinking they were human beings. Afterward he learned that they were angels, and with them he saw God.

And because he loved hospitality, God gave him in return for it a table [?]. For forty years, while the people descended from him were strangers in the desert, God fed them abundantly, because he prepared a table for them in the desert. He gave his children delicacies that produced themselves for forty years in the desert, and he fed the people descended from Abraham because of the table of Abraham's hospitality to strangers. And because the shade of the tree had cooled many poor people, a cloud as shade cooled the people and kept the branches of the God-fearing root safe. And see the wonders, what kind of recompense he paid back: men ate the bread of angels. Indeed, this was rightly very fitting. For Abraham too received angels; because the angels of God ate the food of men, for that reason men also ate the food of angels. For this is how hospitality advances: having received men, it comes to receive angels as well, and from hospitality to angels it comes to be host to God. For it was God who, as a guest, had the angels as his attendants.
That is why our Lord Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, when he spoke about the fruit of the table of those who love humankind, says:
"Whoever receives you receives me." So then the blessed Abraham too received God through his hospitality.
And see the wonderful thing: he saw three, but bowed down to only one. For he did not say, “Lords,” but “Lord.” He saw three, but blessed the one.
But now is not the time to examine that closely, but to present the teaching about hospitality, since he received them and gave them rest.
See the new mysteries of God's love for humankind, what kind of debts the Lover of mankind repays. "I am," he says, "the God of the fathers, who came down from heaven;
you fed the heavenly ones, and I will give the heavenly food to your offspring."
Contrary to the nature of angels, angels ate human food; and beyond the [?] of human beings, human beings partake of heavenly bread.
This food is not familiar to the nature of angels, nor was that food suited to human nature. But now is not the time to present this precisely and [?].

But you, long for a life of hospitality, and strive the good striving for the sake of the poor, so that you may store up treasure for your own soul. You hold the plough handle; sow in the fields of the needy.
"He has scattered abroad," it says, "he has given to the poor [?]; his righteousness endures forever."

Let this much suffice, for this renewed reminder about the poor was not intended as instruction but as confirmation; the things already said at first were enough to encourage those with trained minds.
From now on let us wait for this spiritual father, who is the true teacher of the church. Let us also say to him at the fitting time: "Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp,"
for we are in need of your teaching, and of your fatherly voice to confirm our words. Even if there is much flour, a little leaven is still needed. Even if we have spoken many words,
we still need your fatherly help to lend weight to and confirm our words, to the glory of Christ our God, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
